caption: This image is a digital anatomical illustration depicting the human digestive system within the upper body of a male figure shown from a semi-profile perspective. The main subject is the human gastrointestinal tract and associated organs, visualized through a transparent view of the torso. Key visual elements include the salivary glands highlighted in red near the ear, a pink esophagus leading down to a tan stomach, a reddish-brown liver with a gallbladder beneath it, a pale pancreas stretching horizontally, and the pink and beige coils of the small and large intestines occupying the lower abdomen. There are no visible text labels or words present anywhere in the image. The illustration demonstrates spatial relationships by showing the anatomical sequence of digestion, with the esophagus connecting the mouth to the stomach, which in turn leads into the intestines situated inferior to the liver and stomach.

This is a detailed educational diagram illustrating the human digestive system. The main subject is a profile of a human body showing the internal organs involved in digestion, depicted in shades of pink, orange, red, and yellow against a light beige background. Visible labels on the left side include "Oral cavity," "Mouth," "Submaxillary and sublingual glands," "Liver," "Gall bladder," "Duodenum," "Transverse colon," "Ascending colon," "Ileum," "Caecum," and "Vermiform appendix." Labels on the right side include "Parotid gland," "Pharynx," "Oesophagus," "Stomach," "Pancreas," "Jejunum," "Descending colon," "Rectum," and "Anus." The layout clearly maps out the sequential relationship of the digestive tract, extending from the mouth and pharynx downward through the oesophagus, stomach, small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum), and large intestine (ascending, transverse, and descending colons, caecum, vermiform appendix, rectum) to the anus, with accessory organs like the liver, gall bladder, pancreas, and salivary glands positioned adjacently.

This is a black and white line drawing depicting a single human tooth. The main subject is the tooth itself, shown in profile or side view, oriented vertically with the crown at the top and the long, tapering root extending downward. The visible label consists of a single lowercase numeral "l" (or possibly the number "1") positioned near the bottom right side of the root tip. Key visual elements include the distinct division between the rounded crown section and the elongated root, outlined in thin black lines against a light gray interior fill. The relationship shown is spatial and anatomical, with the crown positioned superiorly directly above the single root segment that ends in a pointed apex.

This image is a black-and-white line drawing or diagram detail showing a single, rounded shape resembling a teardrop or bean. The main subject is this whitish object, which is outlined with a solid black line and has a shaded, textured border on its right side suggesting depth or thickness. There is no visible text, labels, or numbers present anywhere within the frame. The object is oriented diagonally, with its narrower end pointing downward and to the left, connecting to a faint, curving white line at the bottom. No other objects or background elements are shown.

This image is a close-up diagram or text label from an educational document concerning dental anatomy. The main subject consists of two text labels written in a dark serif font against a plain white background. The upper right portion of the image shows the partial word "Can" positioned above and to the right. The lower portion of the image displays the word "Premolars" with a small downward-pointing arrow symbol positioned immediately to its right. The spatial relationship shows "Can" situated above "Premolars," while the arrow points downward and to the right from the end of the second label.

This image is an anatomical illustration showing a top-down view of a human upper dental arch. The main subject is the U-shaped jawbone embedded with distinct, numbered teeth and accompanied by isolated tooth outline sketches in the upper right. Visible labels and text include the partial word "ine" at the top left, alongside numbers 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 8, which correspond to specific tooth positions along the left gum line. Key visual elements feature the cream-colored gingiva holding the white, outlined teeth on the left side, while the right side of the arch depicts cross-sectional or socket views highlighted with pink and red gradients indicating roots. The relationships shown illustrate how the roots of the teeth fit into the alveolar bone of the maxilla, matching the tooth crowns displayed on the opposite side of the diagram.

This is a black and white line drawing depicting a simple, stylized object against a plain background. The main subject is an irregular, folded or layered shape resembling a paper hat or a simple folded paper construction. Key visual elements include clean, dark outlines that define the edges of the form, with some internal overlapping lines suggesting depth or folds. The object is rendered with a light grey fill within its outlined boundaries, and portions of a similar shape appear partially visible at the bottom left. There is no visible text or labels anywhere in the image.

This is an instructional text image that presents a scientific formula on a plain white background. The main subject is the dental formula for adult humans. The text reads in lowercase and serif fonts as follows: "the dental formula in adult humans is I $\frac{2}{2}$ C $\frac{1}{1}$ PM $\frac{2}{2}$ M $\frac{3}{3}$ 32 . The dental". The words "dental formula" are highlighted in a bright cyan color, while the remainder of the text is rendered in black serif lettering. The mathematical fractions and letters represent the various tooth types (incisors, canines, premolars, and molars) relative to their quantities in the human mouth, totaling 32 teeth at the end of the expression.

This is an educational diagram containing two anatomical illustrations labeled "Figure 1.3 L.S. of tooth" and "Figure 1.4 Tongue." The top illustration is a longitudinal cross-section of a tooth showing its internal structure embedded within the jaw bone and gum. It features labels on the left and right pointing to the Enamel, Dentine, Pulp cavity, Gum, Blood Vessels, Nerve, Jaw bone, Periodontal membrane, Crown, Neck, and Root. The tooth layers show enamel on the outermost top surface, dentine underneath, and a central pulp cavity containing blue blood vessels and a yellow nerve. Below this, Figure 1.4 displays an overhead view of a human tongue with labels pointing to Circum vallate papillae, Foliate papillae, Fungiform papillae, and Filiform papillae distributed across its textured surface.

This image is a scientific anatomical diagram illustrating the human stomach and its surrounding structures. The main subject is a shaded pink and peach-colored stomach connected to the esophagus at the top and the duodenum at the lower left. Five primary labels point to different anatomical regions using thin black lines: "Oesophagus" at the top opening, "Cardiac" in the upper right region, "Fundus" in the central body area, "Pyloric" in the lower region, and "Superior portion of duodenum" extending from the lower left outlet. The relationships shown clearly demonstrate the pathway of digestion, with the oesophagus feeding downward into the cardiac and fundus regions, which transition through the pyloric section into the superior portion of the duodenum. The diagram is presented against a plain white background with clean, clear typography.

This is a scientific cross-sectional diagram illustrating the wall layers of the gut. The main subject is a concentric, multi-layered circular structure representing a cross-section of the alimentary canal. The visible text labels are "Serosa", "Muscle layers:", "Inner-circular", "Outer-longitudinal", "Sub-mucosa", "Mucosa", and "Lumen". Key visual elements include concentric rings in various shades of pink and grey, with the outermost layer featuring cell-like oval shapes and the innermost layer presenting a folded, wavy boundary. The layers are arranged concentrically from the center outward: the central white area is the lumen, surrounded by the folded mucosa, then the sub-mucosa, followed by two muscle layers (inner-circular and outer-longitudinal), and finally bounded by the outermost serosa layer.

This image is a text-based anatomical diagram snippet or label set. The main subject consists of three lines of black serif text accompanied by a single horizontal pointer line. The visible text reads "Ducts," "from liver," and "Hepatic ducts," arranged vertically on the left side of the composition. A thin horizontal line extends outward from the left edge of the word "Ducts," serving as a pointer line to indicate a specific anatomical structure. The relationships shown are hierarchical and descriptive, linking the general concept of "Ducts" originating "from liver" directly to the specific anatomical term "Hepatic ducts" positioned beneath them.

This is a medical illustration depicting the anatomical structures of the pancreas, duodenum, and related ducts. The main subject is the pancreas, shown in red with a branching white main pancreatic duct running through its center, partially embraced by the curved, peach-colored C-loop of the duodenum. A green tube, representing the common bile duct, enters from the top and joins with the main pancreatic duct before opening into the duodenal wall. There are no visible text labels or words present anywhere in the image. Two thin black indicator lines extend outward from the diagram toward the left and right margins, but they point to empty space and are not accompanied by any text.

This is a diagrammatic illustration depicting the cross-section of a liver lobule, serving as the main subject. The layout features a hexagonal arrangement with a central purple structure labeled "Central vein" at the core. Radiating outward from the center are cords of pinkish cells labeled "Hepatocytes" and "Hepatic cords," interspersed with blue channels marked as "Sinusoids" and yellow or green networks called "Bile canaliculi." At the outer corners of the hexagonal shape, specialized structures are visible, including blue-shaded vessels labeled "Branch of hepatic portal vein" and red-shaded vessels labeled "Branch of hepatic artery." Pointer lines connect each textual label directly to its corresponding anatomical feature within the lobule cross-section.

This image is a biochemical pathway diagram displaying three horizontal reaction steps against a plain white background. The main subject is the enzymatic activation of pancreatic zymogens. The visible text includes the labels "Trypsinogen," "Trypsin," "Trypsin (Autocatalysis)," "Chymotrypsinogen," and "Chymotrypsin," along with the catalyst labels "Enterokinase" and "Trypsin" positioned above the arrows. Key visual elements consist of three horizontal black arrows pointing from left to right, representing chemical conversions. The relationships shown are that enterokinase converts trypsinogen into trypsin, trypsin can convert trypsinogen into trypsin via autocatalysis, and trypsin also converts chymotrypsinogen into chymotrypsin.

This is an educational text-and-flowchart diagram illustrating the step-by-step breakdown of fats. The main subject is the enzymatic and physical conversion of dietary fats into smaller molecular components. The diagram contains three horizontal rows of text connected by right-facing arrows. The visible labels include "Fats," "Emulsified fats," "Diglycerides," "Monoglycerides," "Fatty acids + Glycerol," "Bile salts," and "Lipases." The visual relationships show that fats are converted into emulsified fats by bile salts, which are then broken down into diglycerides and monoglycerides by lipases, and finally split into fatty acids and glycerol by lipases.

This image is a digital graphic illustration featuring geometric shapes. The main subject consists of four interconnected hexagonal shapes arranged in a cluster against a larger orange and blue rectangular background. The top hexagon is light pink, the left hexagon is light green, the right hexagon is orange, and the bottom hexagon is light blue. Each hexagon is outlined with a thin white border, making them stand out against the background. There are no visible labels or text present anywhere in the image. The four colored hexagons touch each other centrally in a diamond-like formation, overlapping the orange rectangular area that is bordered at the top and bottom by horizontal blue bars, which in turn are set against a pale pink backdrop.

This image is an anatomical illustration showing a semi-transparent view of the human respiratory system. The main subject is the upper body of a person, presented from the waist up in a profile-facing-left head orientation combined with a frontal chest view. Key visual elements include the nasal cavity, oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, and two pink lungs encased within a yellowish skeletal rib cage. There are no visible labels or text present anywhere in the image. The illustration demonstrates the structural relationship of the respiratory tract, showing how air passes from the nasal and oral cavities downward through the pharynx and larynx, into the trachea, and finally branching into the lungs protected by the ribs.

This is a detailed anatomical illustration depicting the structure of a part of a pulmonary lobule, as indicated by the caption "Figure 1.10 Structure of a part of a 'Pulmonary lobule'" at the bottom. The main subject is the microscopic airway and vascular network of the lungs, prominently featuring a terminal bronchiole at the top that branches down into respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and clusters of rounded alveoli and cross-sectioned alveolar sacs. Key visual elements include interwoven networks of red pulmonary arterioles, blue pulmonary venules, green lymphatic vessels, and pulmonary capillaries wrapped around the alveolar structures. The illustration also shows a surrounding layer of light blue elastic connective tissue that borders the entire lobule. Labels pointing to these components include "Terminal bronchiole," "Pulmonary arteriole," "Lymphatic vessel," "Respiratory bronchiole," "Alveolar ducts," "Alveoli," "Alveolar sacs," "Pulmonary Capillaries," "Elastic connective tissue," and "Pulmonary venule."

This is a diagrammatic illustration of the human respiratory system. The main subjects are the human lungs, trachea, heart, diaphragm, and associated thoracic structures. Key visual elements include the pink-colored lungs, a reddish heart positioned between them, a ribbed trachea leading down from the larynx and epiglottis, and the dome-shaped diaphragm at the base. Visible labels on the left side include "Bronchus," "Cut end of rib," and "Lung," while labels on the right side include "Epiglottis," "Larynx," "Trachea," "Pleural membranes," "Alveoli," "Pleural fluid," "Bronchiole," and a central label "heart." The relationships shown depict the trachea branching into bronchi that enter the lungs, the heart nestled centrally between the lungs above the curved diaphragm, and pleural membranes encasing the lungs within the rib cage.

This educational biological diagram illustrates the mechanics of human breathing in two panels labeled (a) and (b), viewed in a sagittal cross-section. Panel (a) shows inhalation, featuring arrows pointing downward into the red-shaded lung area labeled "Air entering lungs," with the "Diaphragm contracted" showing downward arrows and the "Volume of thorax increased." Panel (b) shows exhalation, featuring arrows pointing upward and out labeled "Air expelled from lungs," with the "Diaphragm relaxed and arched upwards" showing upward arrows and the "Volume of thorax decreased." Both panels depict the spinal column on the right and the "Rib cage" with "Ribs and sternum" on the left, demonstrating how their movement outward and upward in panel (a)—and returning to their original position in panel (b)—relates to breathing mechanics.

This is a biological diagram illustrating the structure of an alveolus and its surrounding blood supply. The main subject is an alveolar cavity filled with air, depicted as a light blue central area surrounded by a thin green cellular layer. Key visual elements include a curved blood capillary filled with pink-colored, oval-shaped red blood cells wrapping around the lower and right sides of the alveolus, with a yellow-shaded intermediate region representing the basement substance. The visible text labels are "Air", "Alveolar wall (one-celled thick)", "Alveolar cavity", "Basement substance", "Blood capillary", and "Red blood cell". The relationships shown demonstrate how the one-celled thick alveolar wall and basement substance form a thin barrier separating the air in the alveolar cavity from the blood cells moving through the adjacent capillary.

This image is a text-based educational caption formatted inside a rectangular box with a light peach background and a thin black border. The main subject of the image is the title and description for an anatomical illustration. The visible text reads "Figure 1.13" in bold serif font, followed by the descriptive text "A section of an alveolus with a pulmonary capillary" in regular serif font. The text is left-aligned and spans two lines across the horizontal box. Although the actual anatomical diagram is not present, this caption establishes a direct relationship indicating that the associated figure illustrates the structural relationship between an alveolus and a pulmonary capillary.

This is an educational text snippet displayed in a simple font on a plain, light background. The main subject of the image is the physiological characteristics of systemic veins. The text at the top reads, "Systemic veins -" followed by "carrying deoxygenated blood" on the next line. Below this descriptive text, two numerical measurements are listed: "pO₂ = 40 mm Hg" and "pCO₂ = 45 mm Hg". The layout presents these gas pressure values as specific properties associated with the deoxygenated blood carried by systemic veins.

This is a scientific educational diagram illustrating gas exchange within the lungs. The main subject is an alveolus, represented as a large, light blue rounded structure at the top, positioned above a capillary vessel. Inside the alveolar space, text reads "Alveolar air", "$\text{pO}_2=104\text{ mmHg}$", and "$\text{pCO}_2=40\text{ mmHg}$". Key visual elements include arrows placed between the alveolar air and the underlying capillary, indicating the movement of gases. Specifically, an arrow labeled "$\text{CO}_2$" points upward from the capillary into the alveolus, while an arrow labeled "$\text{O}_2$" points downward from the alveolus into the capillary.

This image is a simplified, two-dimensional anatomical diagram showing a portion of a vessel wall. The main subject is a cross-section of a tubular anatomical structure colored in pink, with a white interior and outlined in black. A horizontal pointer line extends from the outer wall of the structure to the text label. The label reads "Pulmonary" on the top line and "vein" directly underneath. An arc-shaped arrow starts above the structure and curves downward, with its arrowhead pointing directly at the horizontal indicator line.

This educational diagram illustrates gas exchange between systemic arteries and body tissues. The main subject depicts a pink vessel segment labeled "Systemic arteries (carrying oxygenated blood," positioned above three pink body tissue cells labeled with "Body tissues." Key visual elements include downward-pointing arrows indicating blood flow, as well as directional arrows showing oxygen ($\text{O}_2$) moving into the tissues and carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) moving out of them. Numerical labels list partial pressures as "$\text{pO}_2 = 95\text{ mm Hg}$" and "$\text{pCO}_2 = 40\text{ mm Hg}$." The diagram demonstrates the functional relationship where oxygenated blood supplies $\text{O}_2$ to the tissues while receiving $\text{CO}_2$ waste.

This image is a scientific line graph illustrating an oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve. The vertical y-axis is labeled "Oxyhaemoglobin (% Saturation)" with numeric increments from 10 to 100, while the horizontal x-axis is labeled "PO₂ (mmHg)" with numeric increments from 10 to 100. Three distinct sigmoidal curves are displayed: a solid blue middle line, a green dotted line shifted to the left, and a red dotted line shifted to the right. Text blocks indicate physiological shifts, showing an upward blue arrow for pH, downward black arrow for CO₂, and downward blue arrow for Temp on the upper left near the green curve, and a downward pink arrow for pH, upward black arrow for CO₂, and upward red arrow for Temp on the upper right near the red curve. Dashed and solid gray lines extend from the axes to demonstrate points where PO₂ values (around 40, 50, and 60 mmHg) intersect the curves at approximately 83% saturation.

This image is a two-step chemical reaction diagram rendered in black text and arrows against a plain white background. The main subject is the reversible hydration of carbon dioxide and its subsequent dissociation, catalyzed by carbonic anhydrase. The chemical formulas and ions visible are "CO_2 + H_2O", "H_2CO_3", and "+H^+", while the text "Carbonic anhydrase" appears above two sets of horizontal double-headed arrows. The first set of arrows points left and right between "CO_2 + H_2O" and "H_2CO_3", indicating a reversible reaction. The second set of parallel arrows points left and right between "H_2CO_3" and "+H^+", similarly showing reversibility.

This educational scientific diagram illustrates carbon dioxide transport from body tissues to the lungs. The main subjects are two round red blood cells (RBCs) situated within capillaries, surrounded by body tissue at the top and alveolar space in the lung at the bottom. Visible text labels include "Body tissue," "Co₂ Produced," "Co₂ transport from tissues," "Interstitial fluid," "Plasma within capillary," "Capillary wall," "RBC," "Haemoglobin picks up Co₂ and H⁺," "To lungs," "Co₂ transport to lungs," "Haemoglobin releases Co₂ and H⁺," and "Alveolar space in lung," along with chemical formulas such as CO₂, H₂O, Carbonic anhydrase, H₂CO₃, HCO₃⁻, H⁺, and Hb. Key visual elements feature black arrows indicating the chemical pathways and movement of molecules, showing that carbon dioxide produced in tissues diffuses into a red blood cell where it converts into bicarbonate and hydrogen ions with the help of carbonic anhydrase and hemoglobin, and then reverses the process at the lungs to be released into the alveolar space.

This image is a scientific flowchart diagram illustrating the homeostatic control of breathing. The main subject is the feedback loop that regulates blood pH and carbon dioxide levels in the human body. Key visual elements include a yellow box at the top labeled "Homeostasis: Blood pH of about 7.4," a brown box on the right labeled "Stimulus: Rising level of CO₂ in tissues lowers blood pH (such as when exercising)," and a purple box on the left labeled "CO₂ level decreases, restoring pH to normal." The diagram also features anatomical illustrations of the heart with "Carotid arteries," a brain cross-section showing the "Sensor/control centre: CSF" and "Medulla oblongata," and a rib cage diagram. Grey arrows connect these components in a continuous cycle, demonstrating relationships where a stimulus leads to sensor detection, signaling to the control center, a physiological response by the rib muscles and diaphragm, and finally the restoration of homeostasis. A caption at the bottom reads "Figure 1.16 Homeostatic control of breathing."

This image is a colorful graphic illustration featuring a collection of geometric shapes. The main subject is an arrangement of four distinct hexagons partially overlapping a central orange rectangular block with a bright blue border. Each hexagon has a unique solid color: the top one is light pink, the left one is pale green, the right one is vibrant orange, and the bottom one is light blue. All four hexagons are outlined in a thin white border that separates them from the background elements. The top and bottom hexagons touch the outer edges of the central orange rectangle, while the left and right hexagons are positioned directly within it. There is no visible text or labels present anywhere in the image.
